name: wstunnel
language: Rust (v7+ rewrite; earlier versions in Haskell)
last_commit_or_release_date: Active in 2024-2025; 904 commits on main, ongoing releases per GitHub releases page (checked live, recent activity)
maturity_notes: Actively maintained by a single core maintainer (erebe) with community PRs/forks (567). Project has a real history: started in Haskell, was fully rewritten to Rust in v7.0.0 for maintainability, which is itself a maturity signal (author cared enough to redo it rather than abandon it). Single-maintainer risk exists but project has been running for years with steady releases, static binaries, CI, docs, and sponsor (Service Planet) backing. No signs of abandonment.
popularity_signal: ~7.0k GitHub stars, 567 forks, 56 watchers - by far the most popular of the 4 tools surveyed. Has a dedicated docs site (wstunnel.erebe.eu), a public demo server, and commercial sponsorship. Widely referenced in firewall-bypass/DPI-evasion contexts and mentioned in various 'ngrok alternative' and censorship-circumvention roundups.
infra_lift_on_sveltekit_node: Requires running a SEPARATE compiled Rust binary (wstunnel server) as its own OS process alongside the SvelteKit/Node app - it is NOT an embeddable Node/npm library, there is no way to run its server logic inside our existing Node HTTP process. On the cloud side we would need to: download/pin a wstunnel release binary (or build from source), run it as a systemd service or sidecar container, expose/manage its listening port, handle TLS certs (or rely on its auto-reload/self-signed cert feature), and route traffic between it and our Node app (e.g. wstunnel terminates the tunnel and forwards to a local TCP port that our Node app listens on, or vice versa). This is a genuine second service to deploy, monitor, restart on crash, and keep patched - it does not disappear into our existing process.
client_side_simplicity: Client is a single static binary (no interpreter/runtime needed), unprivileged - just run `wstunnel client ...` as a normal user process. Does not require admin/root and does not create virtual network interfaces (unlike VPN-style tools); it only opens local TCP listeners/forwards on ports the user is allowed to bind (high ports need no elevation). This is very close to ideal for our 'no admin' requirement, but it's still a foreign compiled binary the user must download/trust and keep updated, and we'd have to bundle/distribute per-OS/per-arch binaries ourselves.
loc_estimate_and_admin_burden: Low integration LOC in theory (spawn subprocess, or use as a library via Rust crate - not usable from Node directly), but real burden is operational: packaging and distributing a 3rd-party binary for our Python-wrapped client, running/monitoring/restarting a separate server binary in our cloud infra, managing TLS certs and reverse-proxy compatibility (wstunnel explicitly warns it can be finicky behind Nginx/Cloudflare/HAProxy - a real risk since our SvelteKit backend likely sits behind exactly such infra), and diagnosing issues in a Rust codebase we don't own. Roughly: 1-2 days integration/deployment work, plus ongoing binary-update and incident-response burden indefinitely.
viability_notes: The most mature and popular tool surveyed, with a single static Rust binary client requiring no admin/root and no runtime dependency (Node, Python, etc.) — as lean as a client gets short of reusing an OS-bundled tool like SSH. With the separate-server-process requirement now expected rather than disqualifying, this becomes a top recommendation; the one real caveat is its documented finickiness behind Nginx/Cloudflare/HAProxy, worth testing early against our actual serverless SvelteKit deployment's front door.

name: jprq
license: No LICENSE file found in repo (no explicit OSS license listed on GitHub 'Resources' - treat as unlicensed/all-rights-reserved by default)
last_commit_or_release_date: 363 commits on master; project explicitly announced a major operating-model change 'as of Oct 21, 2023' (members-only hosted service) - no clear evidence of commits/releases after that point found in this check
maturity_notes: Red flags: the maintained hosted service (jprq.io) went members-only/paid in Oct 2023, meaning the free public service is effectively discontinued; project is single-maintainer (azimjohn) funded via 'buy me a coffee'; no license file makes self-hosting/forking legally ambiguous. It IS still described as 'open and free to self-host', so the code exists, but the primary maintained deployment path (hosted SaaS) is now gated, which is a strong abandonment/pivot signal for anyone wanting a drop-in dependency.
popularity_signal: ~1.5k stars, 213 forks, 15 watchers - moderate popularity, positioned explicitly as an 'ngrok-alternative/ngrok-replacement' (per GitHub topics), with install support via Homebrew, Scoop, and AUR, suggesting real historical adoption, but momentum appears to have stalled since the 2023 monetization pivot.
infra_lift_on_sveltekit_node: Requires running a SEPARATE compiled Go binary as a relay/tunnel server (the `server/` package with its own http_tunnel.go and tcp_tunnel.go), independent of and not embeddable in our Node process. We would need to build/deploy the Go server binary ourselves (self-host, since the public jprq.io is now gated), run it as its own service, handle subdomain routing and TLS/wildcard DNS ourselves, and monitor/restart it - functionally identical operational burden to wstunnel but with a smaller, less battle-tested, less-documented codebase and an ambiguous license.
client_side_simplicity: Client is a single compiled Go binary installed via package managers (brew/scoop/AUR) or manual download; runs unprivileged, no admin/root needed, no virtual network interface management - just a CLI that opens a local connection and calls `jprq http <port>` etc. Simple from the end-user's perspective, similar in spirit to wstunnel's client.
loc_estimate_and_admin_burden: Similar to wstunnel in shape: we'd need to fork/self-host the Go server (public service gated), build/maintain that binary in our infra, and write a Node bridge from our SvelteKit backend to the tunnel server. Given no active public maintenance since 2023 and unclear license, ongoing burden includes forking and patching bugs ourselves with no upstream support to lean on. Estimate 2-3+ days integration/hardening plus indefinite self-maintenance of a stale codebase.
viability_notes: Same 'separate relay binary' infra burden as wstunnel but with worse maturity signals: no clear license, apparent stalled development, and its hosted service pivoted to paid/members-only in 2023, meaning we'd be adopting an effectively unmaintained project and would own all future bugfixes ourselves. Not recommended.

name: cactus-tunnel
last_commit_or_release_date: 115 commits on main; recent feature work visible (e.g. 'Bridge Mode Web UI' added recently, requires Node.js >= 22), indicating active/recent development
maturity_notes: Small project (58 stars, 7 forks, 1 watcher) with a single primary maintainer (jeffreytse) but shows real recent feature development (bridge mode web UI, live dashboard, verbose logging, tests via Jest, CI badge for tests passing). Not abandoned, but very small community - classic single-maintainer risk: if jeffreytse stops maintaining it, there's little community depth to pick it up. No large-scale production adoption evidence found.
popularity_signal: Only 58 stars/7 forks - the least popular of the four by a wide margin; published on npm as `cactus-tunnel` with an npm version badge and CI passing badge, listed in a couple of 'awesome-repositories' curation sites, but no major mentions found in broader ngrok-alternative roundups or notable adoption signals.
infra_lift_on_sveltekit_node: This is the standout: it is a pure Node.js/TypeScript package (`npm install -g cactus-tunnel`, or `npm install cactus-tunnel` as a library) built on Express + websocket-stream + pump + winston. Its server mode (`cactusTunnel.Server`) is explicitly importable and instantiable as a JS/TS object (`new cactusTunnel.Server({ listen: {...} })`) - meaning the tunnel-server logic CAN run embedded inside our existing Node/SvelteKit HTTP process rather than as a separate OS binary/process. This directly satisfies our top infra priority: no separate relay binary to deploy/monitor/patch on its own - it's just another dependency in our existing package.json, sharing our Node runtime, our existing TLS termination, our existing deploy/monitoring/logging pipeline.
client_side_simplicity: Client is `cactus-tunnel client <server> <target>`, distributed via npm, so the end-user machine needs Node.js >=22 installed (not a zero-dependency static binary like the Rust/Go tools) but runs as a normal unprivileged CLI process - no admin/root, no virtual network interfaces, no elevated capabilities. It also has a 'bridge mode' where the WebSocket relay can literally run inside a browser tab, which is a novel low-privilege option, though impractical for our headless llama-server use case. Requiring Node.js as a prerequisite is the main friction point versus wstunnel/jprq's zero-dependency static binaries - if our Python client wrapper doesn't already assume Node.js is present, this is an extra install step (still non-admin, but an added dependency).
loc_estimate_and_admin_burden: Lowest integration burden of the four for OUR architecture: the server piece is an importable class we can instantiate directly inside our existing SvelteKit/Node backend (roughly tens of lines of glue code to wire it into our existing HTTP server/auth/routing), no separate process to run, monitor, or restart, no extra TLS/cert management (reuses our existing HTTPS termination). Ops burden reduces to 'one more npm dependency to keep patched' rather than 'a second service in our fleet'. Main downside is small community size means we may need to read/patch its source ourselves for edge cases (small codebase makes this feasible - core logic is a few hundred LOC per its own file layout).
viability_notes: Demoted from its prior top ranking for the same architectural reason: the in-process-embedding advantage is moot on serverless infrastructure. Client requires Node.js >=22, heavier than a static binary. Smallest community of any option surveyed (58 stars), raising long-term maintenance risk relative to sish or wstunnel.

name: tunnelite
last_commit_or_release_date: 71 commits; most recent commit Sep 14, 2026 (very recent, active development including CI/CD fixes, homebrew installation docs, NativeAOT binary versioning) - actively maintained as of this check
maturity_notes: Actively developed right now (commits within days of this check), with real engineering depth: integration tests that spin up the tunnel server and a local app in-process to drive HTTP/SSE/WebSocket/TCP traffic, CI running on every PR, a CD pipeline deploying to Azure App Service, and a published homepage (tunnelite.com). Single-maintainer (cristipufu) project with modest star count, so still carries single-maintainer risk, but shows unusually strong test/CI discipline for its size and very recent commit velocity - lower abandonment risk than jprq or cactus-tunnel despite smaller star count.
popularity_signal: 92 stars, 8 forks, 5 watchers - modest but growing; distributed via NuGet (Tunnelite, Tunnelite.Sdk, Tunnelite.AspNetCore packages) with download-count badges, has its own hosted managed service at tunnelite.com (an 'open-source ngrok alternative'), and offers a first-class ASP.NET Core middleware (`app.UseTunnelite()`) - a notable adoption-friendliness signal for .NET shops, though not directly relevant to our Node/SvelteKit stack.
infra_lift_on_sveltekit_node: Requires running a SEPARATE .NET server process (src/Tunnelite.Server) - it is a C#/.NET codebase built on SignalR/ASP.NET Core, which CANNOT run embedded inside our Node/SvelteKit process; there is no JS/TS interop path. Self-hosting requires: provisioning a .NET runtime (or NativeAOT binary) environment, wildcard SSL cert + wildcard DNS for subdomain routing (explicitly required per README), running/monitoring the ASP.NET Core server as its own service (their own reference deployment uses Azure App Service), and bridging it to our Node backend over HTTP/WebSocket at arm's length. This is the heaviest infra lift of the four for a Node-based team, since it also introduces an entirely different tech stack/runtime to operate (.NET) alongside our existing Node/Python stack.
client_side_simplicity: Client is distributed as a NativeAOT-compiled CLI binary (or via NuGet as `Tunnelite` global tool / `dotnet tool install`), runs unprivileged with no admin/root or network-interface manipulation - conceptually as simple as the Rust/Go CLIs. There's also a `Tunnelite.Sdk` library for embedding tunnel-client logic directly into a .NET app and a `Tunnelite.AspNetCore` middleware for auto-tunneling ASP.NET apps - elegant if the local app were .NET, but our local component is Python/llama-server, so we'd just use the plain CLI binary or the SDK from a wrapped process, gaining no special advantage there.
loc_estimate_and_admin_burden: Highest overall admin burden of the four for our stack: requires standing up and operating an entirely separate .NET/ASP.NET Core service (with its own runtime, TLS/wildcard cert management, DNS, deployment pipeline, and monitoring), that our team would need .NET operational familiarity to run well, on top of our existing SvelteKit/Node infra. Integration LOC on the client side is modest (spawn the CLI or shell out from Python), but cloud-side burden is a full second stack to maintain indefinitely - self-hosting docs literally point to Azure App Service as the reference deployment, implying it isn't trivially portable to arbitrary Node-hosting infra.
viability_notes: Improved relative to its prior ranking: a separate server process is no longer a disqualifier, and its client is a lean NativeAOT-compiled single binary, comparable to wstunnel's static-binary approach. Still the heaviest server stack of the realistic options (a full .NET/SignalR/ASP.NET Core runtime distinct from anything else in our infrastructure, with a mandatory wildcard cert/DNS requirement and a reference deployment pinned to Azure App Service) — a real ops cost even though the client itself is lean.
